name: Dīpāvalī (Diwali)
summary: The autumn festival of lamps, spread over about five days around the new moon of Āśvina/Kārttika and observed across India and the diaspora. Different regions and communities give it different reasons — Kṛṣṇa’s killing of Narakāsura, Lakṣmī’s worship, Bali’s yearly reign, Rāma’s return to Ayodhyā, Kālī’s worship in Bengal, and Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa for Jains — which are recorded here as separate, unharmonised associations. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2025.
details:
Kane (1958) describes Dīpāvalī as not a festival of a single deity but a cluster of about five days with independent items: worship of wealth (13th of the dark half, Dhanteras), Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa’s victory over Narakāsura (14th), the worship of Lakṣmī (new moon), Viṣṇu’s victory over Bali and dice-play (Kārttika śukla 1, Balipratipadā), and the exchange of brotherly and sisterly affection (Bhrātṛdvitīyā). He notes older names: Yakṣarātri in Vātsyāyana’s Kāmasūtra, Sukhasuptikā in the Nīlamata Purāṇa (vv. 505–510) and in Hemādri, and Dīpālikā; the Bhaviṣyottara (ch. 140) gives the fullest description of the four days from the 14th. In Bengal the new-moon night is Kālī Pūjā.

UNESCO’s 2025 inscription describes Deepavali as marking the last harvest of the year and the start of a new year and season, and as symbolising the victory of light over darkness and good over evil; the element is tagged with the concepts “epic poetry” and “diaspora”.

dates.event: earliest textual names (Yakṣarātri in the Kāmasūtra; Sukhasuptikā in the Nīlamata)
dates.label: early centuries CE onward
dates.basis: literary references collected by Kane; the texts’ own dates are uncertain

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 194–209

limits: The festival’s several explanatory stories belong to different regions and periods; none of them is treated here as the original reason.

name: Naraka Caturdaśī
summary: The 14th of the dark half of Āśvina (Kārttika in the pūrṇimānta reckoning), the day before the Dīpāvalī new moon: a dawn oil-bath, a lamp lit for Naraka, and, in the south and west, the celebration of Kṛṣṇa’s killing of Narakāsura. Kane argues that the day was originally named for propitiating Yama against hell (naraka), and that the Narakāsura legend was attached later.
details: Kane: the Bhaviṣyottara prescribes an oil bath at daybreak, whirling apāmārga twigs over the head, tarpaṇa to Yama under seven names, a lamp for Naraka and illuminations in temples and public places; “It appears probable that originally the 14th was called Narakacaturdaśī because Yama was to be propitiated for fear of Hell. Later on the legend about the killing by Kṛṣṇa of Narakāsura, king of Prāgjyotiṣa (Kāmarūpa) … was pressed into service.” In the Deccan people crush a bitter fruit underfoot after the bath, which Kane takes to represent Narakāsura. The Kṛttyatattva calls the day Bhūtacaturdaśī.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 196–198

limits: Kane’s reconstruction of the day’s origin is a scholarly interpretation (class 5).

name: Lakṣmī Pūjā of Dīpāvalī
summary: The worship of Lakṣmī (with Kubera in some digests) on the new-moon night of Āśvina/Kārttika, the central night of Dīpāvalī in much of north and west India; merchants close their old account books and open new ones. The Bhaviṣyottara (ch. 140) and the Nīlamata Purāṇa (Sukhasuptikā) describe the night with lamps everywhere and the driving out of Alakṣmī (ill luck) at midnight.
details: Kane: “There is a popular legend that Brahmā gave to brāhmaṇas rakṣābandhana … as their festival, Dasara to kṣatriyas, Dīvālī to traders and Holikā to śūdras.” The Bhaviṣyottara has the king proclaim “today is the sovereignty of Bali; O people! enjoy yourselves”, and women beat winnowing baskets and drums at midnight to drive out Alakṣmī.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 199–201

name: Kālī Pūjā (Bengal)
summary: The worship of Kālī on the new-moon night of Kārttika in Bengal, Assam and Odisha — the same night on which much of India worships Lakṣmī for Dīpāvalī. Kane notes that in Bengal Kālī is worshipped on this day; McDermott traces its spread as a large public festival in Bengal from the eighteenth century.
limits: The eighteenth-century spread is a scholarly reconstruction (McDermott 2011), not checked here.

name: Balipratipadā
summary: The first day of the bright half of Kārttika, the day after the Dīpāvalī new moon, on which Bali, the asura king sent to the netherworld by Vāmana, is worshipped and said to reign for a day; it is also the day of dice-play (dyūta-pratipad) and, in the north, of Govardhana Pūjā. The Bhaviṣyottara (140.47–73) prescribes drawing Bali with his queen Vindhyāvalī and worshipping him with the mantra “salutation to you, O king Bali, son of Virocana … the future Indra”.
details: Kane connects the day with the Vāmana–Bali story (Brahma Purāṇa 73, Kūrma 1.17, Vāmana ch. 77 etc.) and cites the Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 3.1.26, where one who “recites the story of Bali’s imprisonment or represents it on the stage” is said to make Bali bound (Baliṃ bandhayati) — evidence that the story was dramatised long before the festival texts. The Vāmana Purāṇa calls the day Vīrapratipadā; the Purāṇas say Śiva lost to Pārvatī at dice on this day, hence the custom of gambling.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 199–204

name: Govardhana Pūjā and Annakūṭa
summary: Worship of Mount Govardhana and the offering of a “mountain of food” (annakūṭa) to Kṛṣṇa on Kārttika śukla 1, the day after the Dīpāvalī new moon, recalling Kṛṣṇa’s turning the cowherds from Indra’s worship to the hill and lifting it against Indra’s storm. Central in Braj and in the Puṣṭimārga temples.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, p. 205 (Padma Purāṇa calls it Annakūṭa, per the Smṛtikaustubha); list entry “Govardhanapūjā” citing Harivaṃśa 2.17

name: Bhrātṛdvitīyā (Bhai Dūj / Yamadvitīyā)
summary: The second day of the bright half of Kārttika, closing Dīpāvalī, on which sisters feed and bless their brothers; the Bhaviṣya tells that Yamunā fed her brother Yama on this day, hence the name Yamadvitīyā.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 207–209

name: Holī
summary: The spring festival of the Phālguna full moon: a bonfire (Holikā-dahana) on the full-moon night, followed by the throwing of coloured water and powder. Kane traces the name to Holākā, a usage known to Jaimini’s Mīmāṃsā sūtras (as explained by Śabara) and the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya, and regards it in origin as a spring festival; popular legend explains the bonfire by the burning of Holikā, who tried to kill Prahlāda, while Braj celebrates Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa’s play with colours.
details:
Kane: “Holī or Holikā is a festival of unmixed gaiety and frolics throughout India … One element, viz. bonfire, is present almost everywhere except in Bengal.” The Kāmasūtra (1.4.42) names Holākā, which the Jayamaṅgalā commentary explains as sprinkling with coloured water from horns on the Phālguna full moon. Hemādri quotes a long Bhaviṣyottara passage (ch. 132) in which Kṛṣṇa tells Yudhiṣṭhira of an ogress Ḍhauṇḍhā (Dhondhā) who troubled children in king Raghu’s realm and was destroyed by boys’ noise and a bonfire with rakṣoghna mantras; the next day the ashes are saluted and Kāma is worshipped. Bengal instead celebrates the Dolayātrā (swing festival of Kṛṣṇa). In the Deccan colour is thrown on the fifth day (Raṅgapañcamī).

Kane does not mention the Holikā–Prahlāda story, which is the explanation most widely told today (see char:holika).

dates.label: centuries around the turn of the era (Kane: “at least some centuries before Christ”)
dates.basis: mention of Holākā by Jaimini (as read by Śabara) and in the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XII, pp. 237–241

limits: The antiquity argued by Kane rests on the identification of Holākā with Holī and on disputed dates for the sūtras.

name: Holikā (sister of Hiraṇyakaśipu)
summary: In the legend most widely told for Holī, the sister of the asura king Hiraṇyakaśipu, immune to fire, who sat in a pyre with the child Prahlāda to burn him; she was consumed and Prahlāda survived. The bonfire on the eve of Holī is called Holikā-dahana after her.
details: The Sanskrit vrata literature summarised by Kane explains the Holikā bonfire with a different story — the ogress Ḍhauṇḍhā of the Bhaviṣyottara (char:dhaundha) — and treats Holikā as the name of the festival itself. The textual history of the Holikā–Prahlāda version was not traced in this round.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XII, pp. 237–241

openQuestions: Which Purāṇic or vernacular text first tells the Holikā–Prahlāda episode?

name: Ḍhauṇḍhā (Dhondhā), the ogress of the Bhaviṣyottara
summary: An ogress, daughter of Mālin, who in the Bhaviṣyottara’s account of Holī troubled children in king Raghu’s realm; protected by Śiva’s boon from gods, men, weapons and weather, she could be overcome only by boisterous boys, and died when they lit a bonfire with rakṣoghna mantras on the Phālguna full moon.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XII, pp. 238–239

name: Dolayātrā (Dol Pūrṇimā)
summary: The swing festival of Kṛṣṇa on the Phālguna full moon in Bengal and Odisha, Bengal’s form of Holī: an image of Govinda is installed on a swing in a sixteen-pillared pavilion, bathed and swung, with coloured powder (abir). Śūlapāṇi wrote a Dolayātrāviveka on it, recording the tradition that king Indradyumna began the swing festival in Vṛndāvana. Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas keep the day as Caitanya’s birthday (Gaura Pūrṇimā).

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XII, pp. 239–240

name: Navarātri
summary: The nine nights of the Goddess from the first to the ninth of the bright half of Āśvina (with a spring Navarātri in Caitra), observed across India in regional forms — Durgā Pūjā in Bengal, Garbā and Dāṇḍiyā in Gujarat, Golu doll displays in Tamil Nadu, Dasarā in Mysore — and closing with Vijayadaśamī. The Devī Māhātmya is recited during the nine days.
details: Kane: “From the 1st of Āśvina bright half to the 9th is celebrated the Durgāpūjā festival, otherwise called Navarātra, observed all over India in some form or other.” Some works require both an autumn (Śarad) and a spring (Vasanta) Durgotsava. The Kālikā, Devī and Bṛhannandikeśvara Purāṇas and digests such as Śūlapāṇi’s Durgotsavaviveka, Raghunandana’s Durgārcanapaddhati and Vidyāpati’s Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī prescribe its rites; the Devī Māhātmya (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa chs. 78–90 or 81–93 by edition) narrates the Goddess’s victories.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. IX, pp. 154–187

name: Durgā Pūjā (Bengal)
summary: Bengal’s great autumn festival of the Goddess, worshipped with her children (Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya) in clay images made from Gaṅgā clay, from Mahālayā through the 6th–9th days to immersion on Vijayadaśamī; in Kolkata it has become a city-wide public art festival of community pavilions (pandals). “Durga Puja in Kolkata” was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2021.
details:
UNESCO: in the months before the festival artisans sculpt the images “using unfired clay pulled from the Ganga River”; the eyes are painted on Mahālayā; on the tenth day the images are immersed in the river from which the clay came, so that the festival “has also come to signify ‘home-coming’ or a seasonal return to one’s roots”. Kane notes the congregational and social character of the pūjā and the śabarotsava of the tenth day after immersion.

Bengali tradition frames the autumn worship as Rāma’s untimely awakening (akāla-bodhana) of the Goddess before his battle with Rāvaṇa — an episode found in Kṛttivāsa’s Bengali Rāmāyaṇa and in late Purāṇic texts, but not in the Devī Māhātmya or in Vālmīki (see cmp:durga-puja-vs-devi-mahatmya).

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. IX, pp. 154–187

name: Vijayadaśamī (Dasarā / Dussehra)
summary: The tenth of the bright half of Āśvina, the day after Navarātri, one of the three most auspicious days of the year: worship of the goddess Aparājitā and of the śamī tree, crossing the village boundary (sīmollaṅghana), worship of weapons and tools, and — in north India — the burning of Rāvaṇa’s effigy at the end of the Rāmlīlā. In Bengal it is the day of Durgā’s immersion (Bijayā).
details: Kane: Hemādri and the Nirṇayasindhu quote Kaśyapa that “since Rāma started on his invasion (against Rāvaṇa) on Śravaṇa-nakṣatra, men should celebrate the crossing of the limits of their village on that day”. A late verse addressed to the śamī says it “held (concealed) the arrows of Arjuna and … appealed lovingly to Rāma”, alluding to the Pāṇḍavas’ hiding their weapons in a śamī tree before their year incognito (Virāṭaparvan). “In some parts of Northern India Rāmalīlā celebrations go on for ten days and culminate on the 10th of Āśvina in the burning of a tall hollow paper and wickerwork structure concealing crackers representing Rāvaṇa and his hosts.” Former princely states such as Mysore and Baroda held durbars and processions; Kane inclines to a military origin (the season for campaigns) and cites Raghuvaṃśa 4.24–25 for the autumn lustration of horses (nīrājana).

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 188–194

name: Mysore Dasarā
summary: The ten-day royal Dasarā of Mysore (Karnataka), centred on the goddess Cāmuṇḍeśvarī of Chamundi Hill, who in local tradition killed Mahiṣāsura there; the Wodeyar kings held a durbar and the procession of the goddess on an elephant (Jambū Savārī) closes the festival on Vijayadaśamī. It continues the royal Mahānavamī of the Vijayanagara court.
limits: The continuity with the Vijayanagara Mahānavamī is a commonly stated tradition, not checked here against the Portuguese accounts.

name: Mahāśivarātri
summary: The “great night of Śiva”, the 14th of the dark half of Māgha (Phālguna by the pūrṇimānta reckoning), kept with fasting, worship of the liṅga with bilva leaves and an all-night vigil (jāgaraṇa). The Garuḍa, Skanda, Padma and Agni Purāṇas contain its māhātmya, illustrated by the story of a hunter who, keeping awake in a bilva tree, unknowingly worshipped a liṅga below and won liberation.
details: Kane: “The Garuḍapurāṇa I.124, Skanda I.1.33, Padma VI.240, Agni 193 contain the Māhātmya of the Śivarātri on the 14th of the dark half of Māgha.” In the Garuḍa version (which Kane thinks the oldest) the hunter is Sundarasenaka, a niṣāda king on Mount Abu, who goes hunting with his dog; in the Skanda he is a cruel Kirāta named Caṇḍa. The vrata’s three elements are fast, worship and vigil. Major observances are held at Paśupatinātha (Kathmandu), Kāśī and the jyotirliṅga temples, and in Mauritius at Grand Bassin.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XI, pp. 225–236

name: Kṛṣṇa Janmāṣṭamī
summary: The celebration of Kṛṣṇa’s birth on the 8th of the dark half of Bhādrapada (Śrāvaṇa in the pūrṇimānta reckoning), with a fast and a vigil until midnight, the hour at which the Bhāgavata says Kṛṣṇa appeared to Devakī. In Maharashtra the next day’s Gopāḷkālā includes the breaking of pots of curd (Dahi Handi).
details: BhP 10.3.8: “niśīthe tama-udbhūte jāyamāne janārdane … āvirāsīd yathā prācyāṃ diśīndur iva puṣkalaḥ” — at midnight, when darkness had arisen, Viṣṇu appeared in Devakī like the full moon in the east. Kane discusses at length the digests’ debates over the tithi, Rohiṇī-nakṣatra and the midnight hour.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. VII, pp. 124–143 (Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī section)

name: Rāma Navamī
summary: The celebration of Rāma’s birth on the 9th of the bright half of Caitra, with a fast and midday worship. The Rāmcaritmānas dates the birth to “the holy navamī tithi of the month of Madhu (Caitra), bright fortnight, at abhijit (midday)”, and dates its own beginning to a Rāma Navamī; the constituted text of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Critical Edition narrates the birth without naming a month or tithi.
details: RCM Bāla (after dohā 190): “naumī tithi madhu māsa punītā, sukala paccha abhijita haripriītā”. RCM Bāla (before dohā 34) dates the beginning of the poem to Saṃvat 1631, “naumī bhauma bāra madhu māsā” — a Tuesday Rāma Navamī in 1574 CE. In the GRETIL e-text of the Baroda Critical Edition, VR 1.17.6 says only that Kausalyā bore Rāma “endowed with divine marks, half of Viṣṇu”; the familiar statement of the date (Caitra, navamī, Punarvasu) belongs to the vulgate and is not in the constituted text checked. Kane (ch. IV) treats the Rāmanavamī-vrata as obligatory and open even to caṇḍālas.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. IV, pp. 81–94

name: Gaṇeśa Caturthī
summary: The festival of Gaṇeśa on the 4th of the bright half of Bhādrapada, when a clay image is installed, worshipped for one to ten days and immersed in water. Kane treats the domestic vrata in ch. VIII of his History; in Maharashtra Bal Gangadhar Tilak promoted a public (sārvajanik) form from 1893, which became a mass civic festival.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. VIII, pp. 144–153

limits: Kane’s chapter on the domestic vrata was located in the text but its details were not excerpted here.

name: Sārvajanik Gaṇeśotsav (public Gaṇeśa festival)
summary: The public, neighbourhood-organised form of Gaṇeśa Caturthī with large images in street pavilions and processions to immersion, promoted by Bal Gangadhar Tilak in Pune from 1893 as a vehicle of Hindu mobilisation and nationalist politics; it spread through Maharashtra and to Mumbai, Hyderabad and the diaspora.
limits: Public Gaṇeśa images in Pune predate 1893 in some accounts; Tilak’s role was promotion and politicisation rather than invention.

name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
summary: Marathi nationalist leader, journalist and scholar (1856–1920), editor of Kesari, who from 1893 promoted public Gaṇeśa festivals and from 1895 the Śivājī festival in Maharashtra; also author of The Orion (1893) and The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903) on Vedic chronology.

name: Makara Saṅkrānti
summary: The day the sun is reckoned to enter Capricorn (Makara), about 14 January in traditional almanacs, kept with bathing, gifts of sesame and sugarcane and, in Gujarat, kite-flying (Uttarāyaṇ); it corresponds to Pongal in Tamil Nadu and Māgh Bihu in Assam. Kane notes that the traditional date lags the true winter solstice (21 December) by about twenty-three days because of the precession of the equinoxes.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XI, pp. 211–225

name: Gaṅgāsāgar Melā
summary: The pilgrimage and bathing fair at the mouth of the Hooghly on Sagar Island (West Bengal) at Makara Saṅkrānti, where tradition places the hermitage of Kapila and the descent of the Gaṅgā that freed the ashes of Sagara’s sons.

name: Pongal (Tai Pongal)
summary: The Tamil harvest festival at the beginning of the month of Tai (mid-January), named after the dish of new rice boiled over in milk and offered to the Sun; it runs over three or four days — Bhōgi, Pongal, Māṭṭu Pongal (for cattle) and Kāṇum Pongal. Kane notes that it corresponds to the Makara Saṅkrānti of northern and western India and lasts three days.

name: Onam
summary: The harvest festival of Kerala in the month of Ciṅṅam (August–September), culminating on Tiruvōṇam with floral carpets (pūkkaḷam), the feast (sadya), boat races and the Pulikaḷi; Malayali tradition holds that it welcomes the annual return of the just asura king Mahābali, sent to the netherworld by Vāmana. The earliest Tamil reference, in the Caṅkam poem Maduraikkāñci, instead calls Ōṇam the day of Māyōṉ (Viṣṇu) who overcame the asuras.
details: Maduraikkāñci 590–591 (Project Madurai e-text): “kaṇaṅkoḷ avuṇark kaṭanta polantār / māyōṉ mēya ōṇa naṉṉāḷ” — “the good day of Ōṇam that belongs to Māyōṉ of the golden garland, who overcame the crowding asuras”, describing a festival in Pāṇḍya Madurai, not Kerala. Tiruvōṇam (Śravaṇa) is also Viṣṇu’s (Vāmana’s) birth-asterism in Vaiṣṇava tradition. The Kerala story of Mahābali’s welcome is the dominant modern explanation; its literary history is compared with the Purāṇic Bali in cmp:onam-mahabali-vs-puranic-bali.
limits: The Maduraikkāñci line attests a festival named Ōṇam in early Tamil Madurai; it does not show that this is the same festival as modern Kerala Onam or date the Mahābali legend.

name: Maduraikkāñci
summary: A Caṅkam poem of 782 lines by Māṅkuṭi Marutaṉār, one of the Ten Idylls (Pattuppāṭṭu), addressed to the Pāṇḍya king Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ and describing a day and night in Madurai; it contains the earliest known mention of the Ōṇam festival (lines 590–591).

name: Chhaṭh Pūjā
summary: A festival of the Sun (Sūrya) and of the goddess Chhaṭhī Maiyā kept chiefly in Bihar, Jharkhand, eastern Uttar Pradesh and the Nepal Tarai on the 6th of the bright half of Kārttika, six days after Dīpāvalī: after days of fasting, worshippers stand in rivers and ponds to offer arghya to the setting and then the rising sun. It has travelled with Bhojpuri- and Maithili-speaking migrants to Indian cities and the diaspora.

name: Chhaṭhī Maiyā
summary: The mother goddess worshipped with the Sun at Chhaṭh in Bihar and neighbouring regions, regarded as a protector of children; often identified in modern accounts with Ṣaṣṭhī, the goddess of the sixth day after birth, and sometimes called the Sun’s sister or consort.
limits: Identifications vary between local tellings and are not settled by any text checked here.

name: Ratha Yātrā of Puri
summary: The chariot festival of Jagannātha at Puri on the second day of the bright half of Āṣāḍha: Jagannātha, Balabhadra and Subhadrā are drawn on three newly built wooden chariots along the Bada Danda to the Guṇḍicā temple and back after nine days. The Gajapati king sweeps the chariots (chera pahanra). Caitanya’s ecstatic dancing before the chariots is a central scene of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

name: Thaipusam
summary: The Tamil festival of Murukaṉ on the Pūcam asterism of the month of Tai (January–February), when devotees carry kāvaṭi burdens, milk pots and lances piercing the body in fulfilment of vows; tradition says it commemorates Pārvatī’s gift of the vēl (lance) to Murukaṉ for his war against the asura Cūrapatmaṉ. It is kept at Paḻaṉi and other Murukaṉ shrines and, on the largest scale, in Malaysia (Batu Caves, since the 1890s), Singapore and Mauritius.

dates.event: first Thaipusam at Batu Caves, Selangor

name: Kumbh Melā
summary: The “festival of the sacred pitcher”, a mass bathing pilgrimage held in rotation at Prayāga (Allahabad/Prayagraj), Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik, each roughly every twelve years by an astronomical reckoning, so that one of the four falls about every three years; UNESCO calls it “the largest peaceful congregation of pilgrims on earth”. Its primary bearers are the ascetic akhāṛās and āśramas. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2017.
details:
UNESCO: devotees believe that bathing in the Gaṅgā frees them from sins; the congregation includes ascetics, sādhus, kalpavāsīs and visitors; the knowledge is transmitted through “ancient religious manuscripts, oral traditions, historical travelogues” and above all the teacher–pupil relationship of the sādhus in the akhāṛās and āśramas.

Tradition explains the four sites as the places where drops of amṛta fell from the pitcher (kumbha) carried away after the churning of the ocean. Maclean (2003, 2008) argues that the Allahabad gathering was long known as the annual Māgh Melā and acquired the name and twelve-year “Kumbh” status in the nineteenth century, through the Prayāgvāl priests’ adaptation of Haridwar’s Kumbh under colonial administration — “the modern beginnings of the ancient Kumbh Mela” (see claim:kumbh-mela-antiquity).
limits: The amṛta-drop explanation is a tradition; the Purāṇic churning narratives do not name the four sites.

name: The Kumbh Melā is an ancient institution with a continuous history at its four sites
summary: The popular and official view presents the Kumbh Melā as of great antiquity, sometimes citing Xuanzang’s seventh-century account of a great gathering at Prayāga; Maclean argues from colonial and pilgrim-priest records that the Allahabad Kumbh in its present form and name is a nineteenth-century development of the annual Māgh Melā.
details: Xuanzang describes Harṣa’s quinquennial distribution of wealth at the confluence of the rivers at Prayāga, which is not called a Kumbh and is not on a twelve-year cycle; Haridwar’s Kumbh is attested earlier than Allahabad’s. Maclean’s thesis concerns Allahabad specifically.
openQuestions: When is the word Kumbh first applied to the Prayāga gathering in a dated source?

name: Pandharpur Vārī (Āṣāḍhī pilgrimage)
summary: The annual foot-pilgrimage of the Vārkarīs to Viṭṭhala at Pandharpur for Āṣāḍhī Ekādaśī (June–July): hundreds of thousands walk for about three weeks in organised groups (diṇḍīs) singing abhaṅgas, escorting palanquins (pālkhīs) bearing the sandals (pādukās) of the saints — chiefly Jñāneśvar’s from Āḷandī and Tukārām’s from Dehū. A second, smaller vārī falls on Kārttikī Ekādaśī.
details: Irawati Karve’s essay “On the Road” (1962) and D. B. Mokashi’s Pālkhī (trans. 1987) are classic first-hand accounts. A vārkarī is “one who performs the vārī”; the pilgrimage is the defining practice of the tradition.

name: Ayyappa (Ayyappan, Śāstā)
summary: The celibate forest god of Śabarimala in Kerala, worshipped as Dharmaśāstā and as Hariharaputra, the son born of Śiva and Viṣṇu in his female form Mohinī; local tradition also tells of the foundling prince Maṇikaṇṭhan of Pandalam who killed the buffalo-demoness Mahiṣī. His cult draws millions of male pilgrims each season.
details: Sekar (1992) distinguishes the older Śāstā/Aiyaṉār cult from the Pandalam Ayyappa legend and the modern pilgrimage cultus; the identification of Ayyappa with the Tamil village guardian Aiyaṉār is a scholarly and devotional association, not an identity.
limits: The Mohinī–Śiva parentage is a tradition of the cult (later Sanskrit māhātmyas and Malayalam songs), not a Purāṇic narrative of the major Purāṇas checked here.

name: Śabarimala pilgrimage
summary: The season-long pilgrimage (mid-November to January) to the hill shrine of Ayyappa at Śabarimala in the Western Ghats of Kerala. Pilgrims keep a 41-day vow (vratam) of celibacy, vegetarian diet and black or blue dress, address one another as “Ayyappa”, and climb carrying the irumuḍi bundle of offerings; the season culminates at Makaravilakku (Makara Saṅkrānti). Many visit the shrine of Vāvar, a Muslim companion of Ayyappa, at Erumeli on the way.
details: Osella and Osella (2003) analyse the pilgrimage as a rite of masculinity in which men temporarily become renouncers. Customary exclusion of women aged about 10–50 from the shrine was set aside by India’s Supreme Court in 2018 (Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala), a ruling referred to a larger bench in 2019; the matter remained contested.
limits: Legal developments are summarised from reference sources only.

name: Kāṁvaṛ (Kāvaḍ) Yātrā
summary: The pilgrimage of the month of Śrāvaṇa in which devotees of Śiva (kāṁvaṛiyās), dressed in saffron, carry Gaṅgā water in pots slung from a shoulder pole (kāṁvaṛ) — from Haridwar, Gaumukh or Sultanganj — on foot to pour over the liṅgas of their home temples or of Baidyanāth at Deoghar. It has grown since the 1980s into one of the largest annual pilgrimages in north India.

name: Garbā of Gujarat
summary: The ritual and devotional circle dance of Gujarat performed during Navarātri around a perforated earthenware pot lit with an oil lamp (garbo) or an image of the mother goddess Ambā, moving counter-clockwise while singing and clapping, slow at first and building to whirling. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2023.

name: Yoga (UNESCO living-heritage element)
summary: The practice of yoga as a living tradition — postures, meditation, controlled breathing and chanting aimed at self-realisation and liberation — inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2016 on India’s nomination. UNESCO describes it as traditionally transmitted from guru to disciple and now also through āśramas, schools and media worldwide.
limits: This record is the heritage element as inscribed; the philosophical school of Yoga and its texts belong to the darśana records.

name: Muṭiyēṯṯu
summary: A ritual dance-drama of central Kerala enacting the battle between the goddess Kāḷī (Bhadrakāḷī) and the demon Dārika, performed by the whole village after the summer harvest in the goddess temples (Bhagavati kāvus) along the Chalakudy, Periyar and Moovattupuzha rivers; a great image of Kāḷī (kaḷam) is first drawn on the temple floor in coloured powders. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2010.
details: UNESCO: “the divine sage Nārada importunes Śiva to contain the demon Dārika, who is immune to defeat by mortals. Śiva instead commands that Dārika will die at the hand of the goddess Kāḷī.” Each caste has a role in the ritual.

name: Dārika
summary: An asura of Kerala tradition who, by a boon that no mortal could kill him, oppressed the worlds until Bhadrakāḷī, born from Śiva’s third eye, slew him; the story is enacted in Muṭiyēṯṯu and other Bhagavati rituals of Kerala.

name: Kāḷī slays Dārika
summary: The Kerala myth of the goddess Bhadrakāḷī’s war against the asura Dārika, whom no mortal could kill; Nārada informs Śiva, who decrees that Dārika shall die by the Goddess. It is the plot of Muṭiyēṯṯu and of songs and rites in the Bhagavati temples of central Kerala.

name: Rammāṇ
summary: A religious festival and masked ritual theatre held each year in late April in the twin villages of Saloor-Dungra (Chamoli, Uttarakhand) in honour of the village tutelary god Bhūmiyāl Devtā, combining recitation of a version of the Rāma story and other legends with songs and masked dances; only the Bhaṇḍārīs may wear the most sacred mask, that of Narasiṃha. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2009.

name: Bhūmiyāl Devtā (Saloor-Dungra)
summary: The tutelary village god of Saloor-Dungra in the Garhwal Himalaya, in whose honour and temple the Rammāṇ festival is held; the family that hosts the god during the year keeps a strict daily routine.

name: Chhau
summary: A masked and martial dance tradition of eastern India in three styles — Seraikella (Jharkhand), Purulia (West Bengal) and Mayurbhanj (Odisha), the first two masked — enacting episodes from the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa, local folklore and abstract themes, closely tied to the spring festival Caitra Parva. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2010.

name: Saṅkīrtana of Manipur
summary: The ritual singing, drumming and dancing of the Vaiṣṇavas of the Manipur plains, performed at temples, festivals and life-cycle rites: two drummers and about ten singer-dancers narrate the life and deeds of Kṛṣṇa in a hall or courtyard ringed by seated devotees, and the performance is regarded as a visible manifestation of God. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2013.

name: Tradition of Vedic chanting (UNESCO element)
summary: The oral transmission of the four Vedas by memorised recitation with exact accentuation and the mnemonic recitation patterns (pāṭhas), proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003 and inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008.
limits: UNESCO’s summary dates the Vedas to “over 3,500 years ago”; that is the nominating text’s statement, not a dating adopted here.

name: Sbek Thom (Khmer shadow theatre)
summary: Cambodian shadow theatre with two-metre-high, non-articulated puppets cut from a single hide, held up before a fire-lit screen by dancers while two narrators and an orchestra perform scenes of the Reamker, the Khmer Rāmāyaṇa, over several nights with up to 160 puppets. Proclaimed a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed in 2008.
details: UNESCO: dating from before the Angkorian period, it was considered sacred together with the Royal Ballet and mask theatre; many puppets were destroyed under the Khmer Rouge and the art has been revived since 1979.
limits: The pre-Angkorian origin is UNESCO’s (nominating state’s) statement.

name: Lkhon Khol Wat Svay Andet
summary: Khmer masked dance-drama performed by men in the community around the Buddhist monastery of Wat Svay Andet on the Mekong east of Phnom Penh, to propitiate the Neak Ta guardian spirits for the community and its harvest; spirit mediums attend the performance. Inscribed in 2018 on UNESCO’s List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.
limits: UNESCO’s summary does not name the repertoire; the Reamker link rests on reference sources.

name: Three genres of traditional dance in Bali
summary: Balinese dance in its three genres — sacred (wali), semi-sacred (bebali) and for public enjoyment (balih-balihan) — performed to gamelan by male and female dancers in gold-painted costumes, and transmitted informally to children from an early age. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2015.
limits: The names of the three genres are from reference sources; UNESCO’s summary gives them as sacred, semi-sacred and for enjoyment.

name: Geet-Gawai (Bhojpuri folk songs in Mauritius)
summary: A pre-wedding ceremony of Bhojpuri-speaking Mauritians of Indian descent, held at the bride’s or groom’s home, combining rituals, prayers, songs honouring Hindu gods and goddesses, the drum (dholak) and dance; it begins with five married women sorting turmeric, rice, grass and money in a cloth. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2016.

name: Sant tradition (nirguṇa bhakti)
summary: The loose lineage of north and west Indian poet-saints — Nāmdev, Kabīr, Raidās, Dādū and others — who addressed a formless (nirguṇa) Lord, usually named Rām or Hari, through the divine Name and the true guru, and criticised caste, image-worship and ritual. Scholars treat “sant” as a family resemblance rather than an organised sect; Kabīr Panth, Dādū Panth and the Sikh Gurus draw on it.
details: Schomer and McLeod (1987) frame the Sants as a tradition defined by shared teaching and mutual citation rather than by institutions. Songs of Kabīr, Nāmdev and Raidās were collected both in the Sikh Ādi Granth (compiled 1604) and in the Dādūpanthī Pañcvāṇī anthologies of Rajasthan; those collections are referenced here, not modelled.
limits: The sant/saguṇa–nirguṇa division is partly a modern scholarly classification (Hawley 2015).

name: Rāmānanda
summary: North Indian Vaiṣṇava teacher (14th–15th c.), traditionally of Vārāṇasī, revered as founder of the Rāmānandī order; hagiography from the Bhaktamāl onward makes Kabīr, Raidās and others his disciples, which historians treat as a later construction of lineage.

name: Kabīr
summary: Weaver-poet of Vārāṇasī (15th c.), raised in a Muslim julāhā family, the most quoted of the north Indian Sants: his sākhīs, padas and ramainīs address a formless Rām, mock both brāhmaṇ and mullā, and insist on the Name and the true guru. Verses in his name are preserved in three main collections — the eastern Bījak, the Rajasthani (Dādūpanthī) Kabīr Granthāvalī and the Sikh Ādi Granth.
details: Vaudeville (1974) doubted the traditional association with Rāmānanda and saw Kabīr as heir to the Nāth yogis as much as to Vaiṣṇava bhakti. Kabīr’s Rām is not Daśaratha’s son: in the Bījak he repeatedly says the true Rām is unborn and not the king of Ayodhyā (see cmp:kabir-rama-vs-tulsidas-rama). The Sikh scripture includes a large number of verses in his name (reference only).

dates.label: traditionally 1398–1518; scholars place his activity in the 15th c. (c. 1440–1518 on some views)
dates.basis: hagiography (120-year traditional life) vs. Vaudeville’s and others’ estimates

limits: Very little of the corpus can be shown to go back to Kabīr himself; the three recensions overlap only partly.

name: Kabīr Panth
summary: The religious community of Kabīr’s followers, organised in monastic and householder branches (notably the Kabīr Chaurā at Vārāṇasī and the Dharamdāsī branch of central India), which treats Kabīr as the true guru and the Bījak (or the Kabīr Sāgar) as scripture.

name: Bījak
summary: The “Seed” or “Account”: the collection of Kabīr’s ramainīs, śabdas and sākhīs canonical in the Kabīr Panth, representing the eastern (Bhojpuri-coloured) transmission of his poetry.
limits: Attribution of individual verses to Kabīr is uncertain.

name: Kabīr Granthāvalī (Rajasthani recension)
summary: The western collection of Kabīr’s verses transmitted in Dādūpanthī manuscripts of Rajasthan and edited in the twentieth century; with the Bījak and the Sikh Ādi Granth one of the three main recensions of Kabīr.

name: Raidās (Ravidās)
summary: Leatherworker (camār) poet-saint of Vārāṇasī (15th–16th c.) whose songs to a formless Lord reject caste hierarchy; preserved in the Sikh Ādi Granth and the Dādūpanthī Pañcvāṇī, he is revered as guru by the Ravidassia community and, in Rajasthani legend, as Mīrābāī’s guru.

name: Padas of Raidās
summary: The songs attributed to Raidās, transmitted in the Sikh Ādi Granth (about forty śabads), in the Dādūpanthī Pañcvāṇī of Rajasthan and in later collections; edited and translated by Callewaert and Friedlander (1992).

name: Ravidassia (Ravidās Panth)
summary: The community of followers of Guru Ravidās, largely of Dalit (camār) background in Punjab and its diaspora; historically close to Sikh practice, its leading centre, Dera Sachkhand Ballan, proclaimed it a distinct religion in 2010 with the Amritbāṇī of Ravidās as scripture.

dates.event: proclamation as a distinct religion (Dera Sachkhand Ballan)

limits: Members differ on the relation of the community to Sikhism and Hinduism; this record takes no position.

name: Mīrābāī
summary: Rajput princess-poet of Merta and Mewar (16th c.), devotee of Kṛṣṇa as Giridhar Gopāl, whose legend of defiance of her in-laws and of caste and gender norms is told across north India; the earliest datable reference to her is a stanza in Nābhādās’s Bhaktamāl (c. 1600). Hundreds of songs bear her name, nearly all of uncertain authorship.

dates.label: c. 1498–1547 (traditional; married 1516 into the Mewar house)

limits: Hawley (2005) shows that few if any of the poems in her name can be traced to early manuscripts.

name: Padāvalī of Mīrābāī
summary: The large and open corpus of songs (padas) in Rajasthani, Braj and Gujarati attributed to Mīrābāī, addressed to Kṛṣṇa as lover and husband; very few are found in early dated manuscripts.

name: Nābhādās
summary: Rāmānandī poet of Galtā near Jaipur (late 16th–early 17th c.), author of the Bhaktamāl, the “Garland of Devotees”, the first comprehensive hagiographical anthology of north Indian bhakti.

name: Bhaktamāl
summary: Nābhādās’s Braj Bhāṣā “Garland of Devotees” (c. 1600), some two hundred short chappay stanzas on devotees from the mythic past to his contemporaries — Kabīr, Raidās, Mīrā, Sūrdās, Tulsīdās and many others — and the earliest datable reference for several of them. Priyādās’s commentary (1712) expanded it into narrative hagiography.

name: Priyādās
summary: Gauḍīya-influenced poet of Vṛndāvan who completed in 1712 the Bhaktirasabodhinī, a verse commentary on the Bhaktamāl that turned its terse stanzas into the miracle-rich stories of the saints known today.

name: Bhaktirasabodhinī
summary: Priyādās’s Braj commentary (1712) on Nābhādās’s Bhaktamāl, the main source of the popular stories of Kabīr, Mīrā, Tulsīdās and others.

dates.basis: colophon date as reported in secondary literature

name: Dādū Dayāl
summary: Sant poet of Rajasthan (1544–1603), a cotton-carder by tradition, whose followers founded the Dādū Panth; the Dādūpanthīs compiled the Pañcvāṇī anthologies preserving the songs of Kabīr, Nāmdev, Raidās and Hardās with Dādū’s own.

name: Vinaya Patrikā
summary: Tulsīdās’s “Petition of Humility”, 279 Braj Bhāṣā hymns framed as a petition to Rāma’s court, addressed first to Gaṇeśa, Śiva, Hanumān and other deities and then to Rāma; valued for its personal devotion and its theology of the Name.

dates.label: late 16th–early 17th c.
dates.basis: life of Tulsīdās (1574 is the Mānas’s self-dated start)

name: Kavitāvalī
summary: Tulsīdās’s Braj collection of kavitt, savaiyā and other stanzas retelling the Rāma story in seven kāṇḍas, with a long Uttarakāṇḍa of personal and social verses on Kali-age Banaras and the power of Rāma’s name.

dates.label: late 16th–early 17th c.
dates.basis: life of Tulsīdās (1574 is the Mānas’s self-dated start)

name: Gītāvalī
summary: Tulsīdās’s Braj Rāmāyaṇa in songs: 328 padas in seven kāṇḍas set to rāgas, elaborating some episodes and abridging others.

dates.label: late 16th–early 17th c.
dates.basis: life of Tulsīdās (1574 is the Mānas’s self-dated start)

name: Hanumān Bāhuk
summary: A Braj prayer of 44 stanzas to Hanumān, traditionally composed by Tulsīdās in old age when he suffered acute pain in his arm (c. 1607).

dates.label: early 17th c. (traditionally c. 1607)
dates.basis: life of Tulsīdās (1574 is the Mānas’s self-dated start)

name: Vallabha (Vallabhācārya)
summary: Telugu brāhmaṇ teacher (1478–1530) who founded the Puṣṭimārga (“path of grace”) devoted to the child Kṛṣṇa as Śrīnāthjī of Govardhana, and taught Śuddhādvaita (“pure non-dualism”) in his commentaries on the Brahmasūtra (Aṇubhāṣya) and the Bhāgavata (Subodhinī).

name: Viṭṭhalnāth (Gusāiṃjī)
summary: Younger son and successor of Vallabha (1515–1586) who organised the Puṣṭimārga’s temple liturgy of eight daily darśans and, by tradition in 1565, named eight poets — the Aṣṭachāp — whose songs were to be sung in it.

name: Aṣṭachāp (the “eight seals”)
summary: The eight poet-singers recognised by Viṭṭhalnāth as the authorised singers of the Puṣṭimārga liturgy at the Śrīnāthjī temple on Govardhana: Sūrdās, Kumbhandās, Paramānanddās and Kṛṣṇadās (counted as Vallabha’s disciples) and Nanddās, Chītasvāmī, Govindasvāmī and Caturbhujdās (Viṭṭhalnāth’s). Their padas form the core of havelī saṅgīt.
limits: The grouping and the poets’ biographies come from the sect’s Vārtā literature (17th c.); Hawley questions Sūrdās’s membership (claim:surdas-disciple-of-vallabha).

name: Kumbhandās
summary: Farmer-poet of Jamunavato near Govardhana, the earliest of Vallabha’s disciples among the Aṣṭachāp; Puṣṭimārga hagiography tells that he refused the emperor’s summons to Fatehpur Sikri.

name: Paramānanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet from Kannauj, a disciple of Vallabha, whose Braj padas on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood are collected as the Paramānandsāgar.

name: Kṛṣṇadās (Aṣṭachāp)
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet of Gujarati origin and long-time manager (adhikārī) of the Śrīnāthjī temple under Vallabha and Viṭṭhalnāth.

name: Nanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, disciple of Viṭṭhalnāth, celebrated for the refined Braj of his Rāspañcādhyāyī and Bhramargīt, which recast Bhāgavata episodes.

name: Chītasvāmī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, a Mathurā Caube priest who became Viṭṭhalnāth’s disciple.

name: Govindasvāmī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet and musician, a disciple of Viṭṭhalnāth, who lived near Govardhana.

name: Caturbhujdās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, son of Kumbhandās and a disciple of Viṭṭhalnāth.

name: Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā
summary: The Braj prose “Accounts of Eighty-four Vaiṣṇavas”, Puṣṭimārga hagiographies of Vallabha’s disciples (including Sūrdās and the other early Aṣṭachāp poets), attributed to Gokulnāth and transmitted with Harirāy’s commentary (17th c.).

name: Rūpa Gosvāmī
summary: Senior of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvan (1489–1564), a former minister of the Bengal sultanate who met Caitanya at Prayāga; in the Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu and Ujjvalanīlamaṇi he recast Sanskrit aesthetic theory (rasa) as a theology of devotion, and wrote the Kṛṣṇa dramas Vidagdhamādhava and Lalitamādhava.

name: Sanātana Gosvāmī
summary: Elder brother of Rūpa and one of the Six Gosvāmīs (1488–1558), instructed by Caitanya at Vārāṇasī according to the Caitanya Caritāmṛta; author of the Bṛhadbhāgavatāmṛta and a commentary on the Bhāgavata’s tenth book, and traditionally of the ritual code Haribhaktivilāsa.

name: Jīva Gosvāmī
summary: Nephew of Rūpa and Sanātana and the systematic theologian of the Gauḍīya school (c. 1513–c. 1598), author of the six Sandarbhas, which ground Caitanya’s teaching in the Bhāgavata, and founder of the Rādhā-Dāmodara temple in Vṛndāvan.

name: Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
summary: One of the Six Gosvāmīs (1503–1578), from a Śrīvaiṣṇava family of Śrīraṅgam, traditionally co-author of the Haribhaktivilāsa and founder of the Rādhāramaṇa temple in Vṛndāvan.

name: Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
summary: One of the Six Gosvāmīs (1505–1579), remembered as a reciter of the Bhāgavata in Vṛndāvan.

name: Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī
summary: One of the Six Gosvāmīs, a renunciant son of a wealthy Bengali family who lived for years at Rādhākuṇḍa; his memories of Caitanya’s last years at Puri are a main source for Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

name: Works of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvan
summary: The Sanskrit theological, ritual, aesthetic and dramatic works of Rūpa, Sanātana, Jīva and their colleagues (16th c.) that define Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava doctrine and practice.

name: Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu
summary: Rūpa Gosvāmī’s Sanskrit “Ocean of the Nectar of Devotional Rasa”, which classifies devotion (bhakti) and its emotions with the categories of Sanskrit poetics, making bhakti itself the supreme rasa. Its closing verse says it was completed while the author dwelt in Gokula, in a Śaka year given by a word-numeral.
details: GRETIL e-text (Gaudiya Grantha Mandir, based on the 1984 reprint of Haridās Dās’s edition), closing verse: “rāmāṅga-śatru-gaṇite śāke gokulam adhiṣṭhitenāyam / bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhur viṭaṅkitaḥ kṣudra-rūpeṇa”. The commonly cited date 1541 depends on reading the third word-numeral as śakra (= 14).

dates.label: 1541 CE (Śaka 1463)
dates.basis: colophon chronogram as read by Haberman (“rāmāṅga-śakra” = 1463); the GRETIL e-text reads “rāmāṅga-śatru”

openQuestions: Which manuscripts read śakra and which śatru in the colophon?

name: Ujjvalanīlamaṇi
summary: Rūpa Gosvāmī’s Sanskrit treatise on the erotic mode of devotion (madhura-rasa), a sequel to the Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, which classifies Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds and makes Rādhā, with Candrāvalī, the chief of his eternal beloveds in Vraja.
details: GRETIL e-text: “rādhā-candrāvalī-mukhyāḥ proktāḥ nitya-priyā vraje” and “rādhāyām eva kṛṣṇasya suprasiddhānukūlatā”.

name: Haribhaktivilāsa
summary: The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava ritual digest (16th c.) on initiation, daily worship, festivals and conduct, attributed to Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī with a commentary ascribed to Sanātana.

name: Ṣaṭ Sandarbha
summary: Jīva Gosvāmī’s six “Treatises” (Tattva-, Bhagavat-, Paramātma-, Kṛṣṇa-, Bhakti- and Prīti-sandarbha), a systematic theology of the Gauḍīya school built on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

name: Vṛndāvana Dāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Bengali poet (1507–1589), disciple of Nityānanda, whose Caitanya Bhāgavata is the first full-length Bengali biography of Caitanya.

name: Caitanya Bhāgavata
summary: Vṛndāvana Dāsa’s Bengali verse biography of Caitanya (16th c.), the earliest full-length life in Bengali, concentrating on his youth in Navadvīpa and his early ministry; it presents him as Kṛṣṇa (and Rādhā) descended.

name: Śikṣāṣṭaka
summary: Eight Sanskrit verses of instruction on the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s names, humility and longing, attributed to Caitanya and quoted in the last chapter of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta; the only verses Gauḍīyas ascribe to him directly.

name: Śākta Padāvalī (Bengali songs to the Goddess)
summary: The Bengali song literature to Kālī and Umā from the eighteenth century onward — Śyāmā-saṅgīt to Kālī and the Āgamanī–Bijayā songs of Umā’s homecoming at Durgā Pūjā — initiated by Rāmprasād Sen and Kamalākānta Bhaṭṭācārya.

name: Rāmprasād Sen
summary: Bengali Śākta poet of Halisahar (c. 1718/1723–c. 1775) whose intimate, often reproachful songs to Kālī as mother (Rāmprasādī) created the genre of Śyāmā-saṅgīt; patronised by Rājā Kṛṣṇacandra of Nadia, who gave him the title Kavirañjana.

name: Kamalākānta Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: Bengali Śākta poet and tantric practitioner (1769–1821), court poet of the Mahārājā of Burdwan, who after Rāmprasād shaped the Śākta padāvalī, including the Āgamanī songs of Umā’s homecoming.

name: Baḍu Caṇḍīdās
summary: Bengali poet to whom the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan is ascribed (late 14th–15th c.?). Songs signed “Caṇḍīdās” — with the epithets Baḍu, Dvija and Dīna — appear to belong to more than one poet, a puzzle known as the Caṇḍīdās problem.

dates.label: 14th–15th c. (disputed)
dates.basis: language of the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan; disputed identity

name: Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan
summary: A Bengali dramatic song-cycle of the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa ascribed to Baḍu Caṇḍīdās, known from a single incomplete manuscript found in the early twentieth century in a cowshed in Bankura district and published by the Bangiya Sahitya Parishad; among the earliest monuments of Middle Bengali.

dates.label: later 14th–15th c. (pre-Caitanya; disputed)
dates.basis: language; palaeography of the unique manuscript

limits: The date and the relationship of this Caṇḍīdās to the lyric Caṇḍīdās poems are unsettled.

name: Vidyāpati
summary: Maithili and Sanskrit poet, scholar and courtier of the Oinwāra kings of Mithilā (c. 1352–1448), whose Maithili songs of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa were taken up by Bengali Vaiṣṇavas (and imitated in Brajabuli), while his songs to Śiva (nacārī) and his Sanskrit works on Durgā worship show a Smārta devotion to several deities.

dates.label: c. 1352–1448
dates.basis: court records and colophons as reported

name: Padāvalī of Vidyāpati
summary: The Maithili love-songs (padas) of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and songs to Śiva and the Goddess attributed to Vidyāpati, transmitted in Mithilā, Nepal and Bengal; Caitanya is said to have delighted in them.

name: Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī
summary: Vidyāpati’s Sanskrit manual of the autumn worship of Durgā, cited by Kane among the special treatises on the Durgotsava/Navarātra.

name: Nām Ghoṣā
summary: Mādhavadeva’s Assamese “Proclamation of the Name”, about a thousand verses in praise of the Name of Kṛṣṇa (Rāma/Hari), with Śaṅkaradeva’s Kīrtana Ghoṣā a principal scripture of the Ekaśaraṇa sattras and nāmghars.

name: Bargīt
summary: The “great songs” of Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva (15th–16th c.) in Brajāvalī, set to rāgas but not necessarily to tāla, sung to open services in the sattras and nāmghars of the Ekaśaraṇa Dharma.

name: Aṅkīyā Nāṭ and Bhāonā
summary: The one-act devotional plays in Brajāvalī created by Śaṅkaradeva in the early sixteenth century, mostly on Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, and their performance (bhāonā) in the nāmghars and sattras of Assam, directed and narrated by a sūtradhāra.

name: Sattriya
summary: The dance tradition of the Ekaśaraṇa sattras, created within the bhāonā performances of Śaṅkaradeva’s plays and maintained by celibate monks; recognised among India’s classical dances by the Sangeet Natak Akademi in 2000.

dates.event: recognition as a classical dance (Sangeet Natak Akademi)
dates.label: 15 November 2000

name: Sattra (Vaiṣṇava monasteries of Assam)
summary: The monastic and congregational institutions of the Ekaśaraṇa Dharma — chiefly on Majuli and in upper Assam — that preserve its scriptures, Bargīt, plays and dance under a sattrādhikār.

name: Pañcasakhā (the “five friends” of Odia literature)
summary: The five sixteenth-century Odia poet-saints — Balarāma Dāsa, Jagannātha Dāsa, Acyutānanda Dāsa, Yaśovanta Dāsa and Ananta Dāsa — who rendered Sanskrit scriptures into Odia and joined Jagannātha devotion with a meditative, nirguṇa-leaning Vaiṣṇavism, sometimes called Utkalīya Vaiṣṇavism.

name: Balarāma Dāsa
summary: Eldest of the Odia Pañcasakhā, author of the Jagamohana (Dāṇḍi) Rāmāyaṇa, the Lakṣmī Purāṇa and the Bhakti-tattva of the “Bata Abakasha”; tradition calls him Krupāsiddha.

name: Acyutānanda Dāsa
summary: Odia Pañcasakhā poet and saint, prolific author of Mālikās (prophetic verses), genealogical and devotional works, and a figure of popular prophecy in Odisha.

name: Yaśovanta Dāsa
summary: Odia Pañcasakhā poet, remembered for devotional and yogic songs (the Prema Bhakti Brahma Gītā and Mālikās are attributed to him).

name: Ananta Dāsa
summary: Odia Pañcasakhā poet, author by tradition of the Hetu-udaya Bhāgavata and devotional songs.

name: Jagamohana Rāmāyaṇa (Dāṇḍi Rāmāyaṇa)
summary: Balarāma Dāsa’s Odia Rāmāyaṇa (early 16th c.), in the popular dāṇḍi metre, a free retelling rather than a translation of Vālmīki, long recited in Odisha’s village prayer-houses.

name: Janābāī
summary: Marathi Vārkarī poet-saint (d. 1350 by tradition), a low-caste orphan who served as a maid in Nāmdev’s household at Pandharpur; her abhaṅgas address Viṭṭhal with startling intimacy as mother, friend and helper in her chores.

name: Muktābāī
summary: Younger sister of Jñāneśvar (13th c.) and Vārkarī poet of about forty abhaṅgas, remembered in tradition as the teacher of the yogī Cāṅgdev.

name: Cokhāmeḷā
summary: Vārkarī poet-saint of the Mahār (untouchable) caste (13th–14th c.), of Mangalvedhe, a companion of Nāmdev; barred from the Viṭṭhal temple, he sang of the god outside it, and his samādhi lies at the foot of the temple steps in Pandharpur. He is a key figure for modern Dalit memory.

name: Bahiṇābāī
summary: Marathi Vārkarī poet-saint (1628–1700), a brāhmaṇ woman who took Tukārām as her guru in a vision and whose autobiography in abhaṅgas (Ātmanivedana) records the conflict of devotion with her married life.

name: Samarth Rāmdās
summary: Marathi saint (c. 1608–1682), devotee of Rāma and Hanumān, founder of the Rāmdāsī order and of Hanumān shrines across Maharashtra, author of the Dāsbodh and the Manāce Ślok; later tradition makes him guru to the Maratha king Śivājī.

name: Dāsbodh
summary: Rāmdās’s Marathi “Advice to the Servant” (1654), 7,751 ovīs in twenty chapters of ten sub-chapters each, a dialogue of guru and disciple on devotion, knowledge and worldly conduct, dictated to his disciple Kalyāṇ Svāmī.

name: Manāce Ślok
summary: Rāmdās’s 205 Marathi verses “to the mind”, a widely memorised didactic poem urging the mind toward Rāma.

name: Vaiṣṇava jana to
summary: Narsinh Mehtā’s Gujarati pad defining the true devotee of Viṣṇu by ethical conduct — feeling others’ pain, humility, freedom from greed — rather than caste or ritual; it was sung daily in Gandhi’s āśrams.

name: Premānand Bhaṭṭ
summary: Gujarati poet and professional storyteller (māṇbhaṭ, 1636–1714) of Vadodara, master of the ākhyāna — sung narratives of Purāṇic and bhakti stories such as Okhāharaṇ, Nalākhyān and Sudāmā-caritra, and of Narsinh Mehtā’s life.

name: Swaminarayan (Sahajānand Svāmī)
summary: Ascetic and religious founder (1781–1830), born Ghanaśyām Pāṇḍe near Ayodhyā, who after years of wandering was initiated by Rāmānand Svāmī in Gujarat in 1800 and succeeded him in 1802; his followers worship him as the supreme manifestation of God (Puruṣottama), and the Swaminarayan Sampradāya grew from his reforms.

name: Swaminarayan Sampradāya
summary: A Vaiṣṇava tradition founded in Gujarat in the early nineteenth century around Sahajānand Svāmī (Swaminarayan), rooted in Rāmānuja’s Viśiṣṭādvaita, organised around the dioceses of Ahmedabad and Vadtal and temples built in his lifetime, and spread by Gujarati migrants to East Africa, Britain and North America.

dates.event: succession of Sahajānand Svāmī to Rāmānand Svāmī’s fellowship

name: Vacanāmṛt
summary: The 273 Gujarati discourses of Swaminarayan delivered between 1819 and 1829, compiled by five senior disciples and approved by him; the principal theological scripture of the Swaminarayan Sampradāya.

name: Śikṣāpatrī
summary: Swaminarayan’s code of conduct in 212 Sanskrit verses (1826) for his followers; on 26 February 1830 at Rajkot he presented a copy to Sir John Malcolm, Governor of Bombay, which is now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford.

dates.event: copy presented to Sir John Malcolm (now Bodleian Library)
dates.label: 26 February 1830

limits: The Bodleian copy was not checked in the library’s catalogue here.

name: BAPS (Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha)
summary: A Swaminarayan denomination formed in 1905 by Shastri Yagnapurushdas (Shastriji Maharaj), teaching that Swaminarayan (Puruṣottama) remains present through a succession of gurus who embody Akṣara, beginning with Guṇātītānand Svāmī; known worldwide for its large stone mandirs, including Neasden (London) and Robbinsville (New Jersey).

name: Shastriji Maharaj (Shastri Yagnapurushdas)
summary: Swaminarayan monk and scholar (1865–1951) who in 1905 left the Vadtal diocese to found BAPS around the Akṣara–Puruṣottama doctrine.

name: Haridāsa (Dāsa Kūṭa)
summary: The movement of Kannada devotional singers — “servants of Hari” — within the Mādhva (Dvaita) tradition, from Śrīpādarāja and Vyāsatīrtha to Purandaradāsa and Kanakadāsa and later Vijayadāsa, whose simple Kannada songs (kīrtanas, ugābhogas, suḷādis) carried Dvaita devotion to the people and shaped Carnatic music.

name: Vyāsatīrtha
summary: Mādhva (Dvaita) philosopher and pontiff (1447–1539), rājaguru of the Vijayanagara court under Kṛṣṇadevarāya, author of the polemical Nyāyāmṛta, Tarkatāṇḍava and Tātparyacandrikā, and patron and teacher of the Haridāsas Purandaradāsa and Kanakadāsa.

name: Purandaradāsa
summary: Kannada Haridāsa poet-composer (c. 1484–1564), a wealthy merchant who became a disciple of Vyāsatīrtha; his songs signed “Purandara Viṭhala” and his graded exercises made him the “grandfather” (pitāmaha) of Carnatic music.

name: Kanakadāsa
summary: Kannada Haridāsa poet (1509–1609 or 1606), of the Kuruba (shepherd) community, disciple of Vyāsatīrtha; Udupi tradition says Kṛṣṇa turned to face him through a window in the temple wall (Kanakana kiṇḍi) when he was barred from entering. Author of the Mohanataraṅgiṇi and the allegory Rāmadhānya Caritre.

name: Mohanataraṅgiṇi
summary: Kanakadāsa’s Kannada narrative poem (in sāṅgatya metre) on Kṛṣṇa’s life at Dvārakā, including the love of Uṣā and Aniruddha.

name: Rāmadhānya Caritre
summary: Kanakadāsa’s Kannada allegory in which ragi (finger millet), the grain of the poor, wins a debate with rice before Rāma and earns the name rāmadhānya — read as a protest against caste privilege.

name: Annamācārya (Annamayya)
summary: Telugu composer of Tāḷḷapāka (1408–1503) who sang to Veṅkaṭeśvara of Tirumala; family tradition credits him with some 32,000 saṅkīrtanas, of which about 14,900 survive engraved on copper plates kept at Tirumala, the earliest large body of songs in the kīrtana form.

dates.basis: family copper-plate tradition and biography by his grandson

name: Saṅkīrtanas of Annamācārya
summary: The Telugu (and some Sanskrit) songs of Annamācārya on Veṅkaṭeśvara, in devotional (adhyātma) and erotic (śṛṅgāra) modes, preserved on the Tāḷḷapāka copper plates at Tirumala; translated in part by Narayana Rao and Shulman (2005).

name: Carnatic music
summary: The classical music tradition of south India, built on rāga and tāla and on a repertoire of devotional song (kṛti, kīrtana, padam, varṇam) — from the Haridāsas and Annamācārya to the eighteenth–nineteenth-century “Trinity” of Tyāgarāja, Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri.

name: Tyāgarāja
summary: Telugu composer of Tiruvaiyaru in the Thanjavur country (1767–1847), the most celebrated of the Carnatic “Trinity”, whose hundreds of kṛtis — among them the five Pañcaratna kṛtis — are songs of devotion to Rāma; he is said to have refused royal patronage.

name: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar
summary: Sanskrit-language composer of the Carnatic “Trinity” (1775/76–1835), signing as “Guruguha”; his some 500 kṛtis describe the deities, temples and tantric worship of dozens of shrines, including the Kamalāmbā Navāvaraṇa kṛtis of Tiruvārūr.

name: Śyāma Śāstri
summary: Eldest of the Carnatic “Trinity” (1762–1827), a priest of the goddess Kāmākṣī (Bangāru Kāmākṣī) at Thanjavur, whose compositions are almost all addressed to the Goddess.

name: Pañcaratna kṛtis
summary: Five Telugu kṛtis of Tyāgarāja in the rāgas Nāṭa, Gauḷa, Ārabhi, Varāḷi and Śrī, sung together by assembled musicians at his annual ārādhanā at Tiruvaiyaru.

name: Tyāgarāja Ārādhanā
summary: The annual music festival at Tyāgarāja’s samādhi on the Kāvēri at Tiruvaiyaru on the anniversary of his death (Puṣya bahuḷa pañcamī), culminating in the collective singing of the Pañcaratna kṛtis.

name: Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu (Kañcarla Gopanna)
summary: Telugu devotee-composer (c. 1620–1688), revenue official under the Qutb Shāhī sultans of Golconda, who by tradition spent government money rebuilding the Rāma temple at Bhadrācalam, was imprisoned for twelve years and released when Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa repaid the sum; author of kīrtanas and the Dāśarathi Śatakam.

name: Dāśarathi Śatakam
summary: A Telugu śatakam of about a hundred verses addressed to Rāma, son of Daśaratha, attributed to Kañcarla Gopanna (Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu).

name: Kṣetrayya
summary: Telugu composer of padams (c. 1600–1680) from Muvva in the Krishna delta, whose love songs to Muvva Gopāla (Kṛṣṇa), voiced mostly by courtesans and women, became central to the repertoire of dance (devadāsī and later Bharatanāṭyam).

name: Padams of Kṣetrayya
summary: Several hundred surviving Telugu padams (of thousands attributed) signed with the mudrā “Muvva Gopāla”, translated in part in When God Is a Customer (1994).

name: Akka Mahādēvi
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet-saint of the twelfth century from Uḍutaḍi, who renounced marriage (and, in legend, clothing) for her divine husband Śiva as Cennamallikārjuna, “the lord white as jasmine”, and joined the gathering of Basava and Allama at Kalyāṇa before ending her life on Śrīśaila; some 430 vacanas are attributed to her.

name: Allama Prabhu
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva mystic poet of the twelfth century, presiding figure of the Anubhava Maṇṭapa of Kalyāṇa in tradition, whose enigmatic vacanas to Guhēśvara (“lord of the caves”) criticise ritual and teach the unity of self and Śiva.

name: Vacanas of Akka Mahādēvi
summary: The Kannada free-verse sayings (vacanas) signed “Cennamallikārjuna”, about 430 attributed to Akka Mahādēvi.

name: Vacanas of Allama Prabhu
summary: The Kannada vacanas signed “Guhēśvara” attributed to Allama Prabhu, admired for paradox and riddling imagery.

name: Śūnya Sampādane
summary: A fifteenth-century Kannada anthology that arranges the vacanas of Allama, Basava, Akka Mahādēvi and others as dialogues in the Anubhava Maṇṭapa around Allama, the “attainment of the void”; compiled in several redactions in the Vijayanagara period.

name: Aruṇakirinātar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet of Tiruvaṇṇāmalai (c. 1370–1450 on Zvelebil’s dating), author of the Tiruppukaḻ, rhythmically intricate songs to Murukaṉ at his shrines, and of the Kantar Anupūti and Kantar Alaṅkāram.

name: Tiruppukaḻ
summary: Aruṇakirinātar’s “Holy Praise”, some 1,300 surviving Tamil songs to Murukaṉ in elaborate rhythmic patterns (cantam), arranged by the shrines they praise; the Project Madurai edition numbers the songs 1–1326.
details: The Project Madurai part 1 (songs 1–330) opens with a song to Vināyaka (“kaittala niṟaikaṉi”) and contains songs headed for Tirupparaṅkuṉṟam, Tiruccentūr, Paḻani and Tiruttaṇikai among other shrines (checked 2026-11-08).

name: Mēlputtūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri
summary: Kerala Sanskrit poet and grammarian (1560–1646/1666), author of the Prakriyāsarvasva on Pāṇinian grammar and of the Nārāyaṇīyam, a condensation of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa in a thousand verses addressed to Kṛṣṇa of Guruvāyūr.

name: Nārāyaṇīyam
summary: A Sanskrit devotional poem of 100 cantos (daśakas), 1,034 verses, condensing the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and addressed throughout to Kṛṣṇa of Guruvāyūr (“pavanapurapate”). Its last verse ends with the phrase “āyurārogyasaukhyam”, which as a kali-day chronogram gives a date in 1586 CE.
details: GRETIL e-text, Nār. 100.10: “nityaṃ cittasthitaṃ me pavanapurapate kṛṣṇa kāruṇyasindho”; 100.11 ends “… idam iha kurutām āyurārogyasaukhyam”. The decoding of the chronogram is traditional; the arithmetic is shown in the date basis. Wikipedia notes that the earliest manuscripts are much later than the poem.

dates.label: 1586 CE (kali-day 1,712,210)
dates.basis: kaṭapayādi reading of “āyurārogyasaukhyam” (y=1, r=2, r=2, g(y)=1, s=7, kh(y)=1, read right to left) = 1,712,210 days of the Kali age

limits: The 1586 date depends on accepting the final phrase as an intended chronogram.

name: Pūntānam Nampūtiri
summary: Malayalam devotional poet (1547–1640) of Keezhattoor, devotee of Guruvāyūrappan, author of the Jñānappāna; Guruvāyūr legend contrasts his simple bhakti, which the god preferred, with Bhaṭṭatiri’s learned Sanskrit.

name: Jñānappāna
summary: Pūntānam’s Malayalam “Song of Divine Wisdom” (16th c.), a meditation in simple verse on the transience of life and devotion to Kṛṣṇa of Guruvāyūr.

name: Rāmaliṅga Swāmigaḷ (Vaḷḷalār)
summary: Tamil saint and poet (1823–1874) of Marutūr near Chidambaram, who preached compassion to all living beings (jīvakāruṇyam), founded the Samaraca Cutta Caṉmārka Caṅkam (1865), a free kitchen at Vadalur (1867) and the Sathya Gnana Sabai (1872) to a formless “Arutperuñjōti” (Grace-Light); his collected hymns, the Tiruvaruṭpā, provoked the “Aruṭpā–Maruṭpā” controversy with Śaiva Siddhāntins.

name: Samaraca Cutta Caṉmārkam (Vaḷḷalār’s path)
summary: The universalist movement founded by Rāmaliṅga Swāmigaḷ in 1865, centred on the worship of God as light and on feeding the hungry, with its Sathya Gnana Sabai at Vadalur (1872).

name: Tiruvaruṭpā
summary: The collected Tamil hymns of Rāmaliṅga Swāmigaḷ, arranged in six tirumuṟais, the first parts published in his lifetime (1867); their claim to scriptural status was attacked by Āṟumuka Nāvalar in the “Aruṭpā–Maruṭpā” dispute.

name: Bhānubhakta Ācārya
summary: Nepali poet (1814–1868) honoured as Ādikavi, the first poet of Nepali, for his Nepali Rāmāyaṇa; also known for verse letters and satire written while imprisoned. His birthday (Bhānu Jayantī) is a cultural holiday in Nepal and among Nepali speakers in India.

name: Bhānubhakta Rāmāyaṇa
summary: Bhānubhakta’s Nepali Rāmāyaṇa in seven kāṇḍas, circulated orally and in manuscript and published complete in 1887 by Motirām Bhaṭṭa; regarded as the first Nepali epic and a foundation of the literary language. Hutt treats it as based on the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.
details: Wikipedia’s article calls it a translation of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Hutt (1988) and older Nepali scholarship identify the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa as its source. Both views are recorded.
openQuestions: A canto-by-canto comparison with the Adhyātma would settle the source question.

name: Utpaladeva
summary: Kashmiri Śaiva philosopher and poet (c. 900–950), pupil of Somānanda and grand-teacher of Abhinavagupta, who systematised the Pratyabhijñā (“Recognition”) school in the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā and poured its theology into the devotional hymns of the Śivastotrāvalī.

dates.label: c. 900–950
dates.basis: teacher–pupil chronology of the Kashmir Śaiva lineage

name: Śivastotrāvalī
summary: Utpaladeva’s “Garland of Hymns to Śiva”, twenty Sanskrit stotras of personal devotion grounded in Pratyabhijñā non-dualism, collected after him with a commentary by Kṣemarāja; still recited by Kashmiri Paṇḍits.

sources.locator: Śivastotrāvalī (GRETIL e-text based on Bailly’s edition)

name: Rūpa Bhavānī
summary: Kashmiri Paṇḍit woman mystic and poet (c. 1621–1721), whose Kashmiri vākhs in the line of Lal Ded express Śaiva yogic experience; she is commemorated by Kashmiri Paṇḍits on her birth anniversary (Sahib Saptami).

name: Old Javanese kakawin and parwa literature
summary: The court literature of Java and Bali in Old Javanese: prose renderings of Mahābhārata books (parwa, from the late 10th c.) and long poems in Sanskrit metres (kakawin) retelling epic and Purāṇic stories — Rāmāyaṇa, Arjunawiwāha, Kṛṣṇāyana, Bhāratayuddha, Hariwangsa and others — preserved mainly in Balinese palm-leaf manuscripts.

name: Airlangga
summary: King in East Java (r. 1019–1042), of Balinese birth, who restored the kingdom after the fall of Dharmawangsa Teguh’s court (c. 1016) and is named in the Arjunawiwāha as the poet Mpu Kanwa’s king; his Pucangan inscription of 1041 recounts his career.

name: Mpu Kanwa
summary: Old Javanese poet of King Airlangga’s court (early 11th c.), known only from his Arjunawiwāha, in whose last stanza (36.2) he names himself, the work and the king.

name: Arjunawiwāha (Kakawin)
summary: Mpu Kanwa’s Old Javanese kakawin “Arjuna’s Wedding” (11th c.), the oldest dated kakawin after the Rāmāyaṇa: Arjuna’s ascetic penance, his resistance to the nymphs sent to test him, the fight with Śiva as a hunter over the boar Muka, and his victory for Indra over the demon Niwātakawaca, rewarded with marriage to the nymphs. It retells the Mahābhārata’s Āraṇyakaparvan episodes and remained a favourite of Javanese and Balinese wayang.

name: Jayabhaya (king of Kaḍiri)
summary: King of Kaḍiri (Daha) in East Java (r. c. 1130/1135–1157), known from inscriptions of 1135, 1136 and 1144 under the consecration name Śrī Warmeśwara, patron of the Bhāratayuddha; later Javanese tradition made him a prophet-king (the Jangka Jayabaya prophecies).

dates.label: c. 1130/1135 – 1157
dates.basis: inscriptions of 1135, 1136, 1144 and the Bhāratayuddha chronogram

name: Mpu Sedah
summary: Old Javanese court poet of King Jayabhaya of Kaḍiri, who began the Bhāratayuddha in 1157; Javanese legend that he was put to death for modelling Śalya’s queen on the king’s consort is dismissed by Zoetmulder as having no basis in the text.

name: Mpu Panuluh
summary: Old Javanese court poet who completed the Bhāratayuddha begun by Mpu Sedah and wrote the kakawins Hariwangsa and Ghaṭotkacāśraya (12th c.).

sources.locator: pp. 339–341 and chapters on Hariwangsa and Ghaṭotkacāśraya

name: Bhāratayuddha (Kakawin)
summary: The Old Javanese kakawin of the Mahābhārata war, begun by Mpu Sedah and completed by Mpu Panuluh for King Jayabhaya of Kaḍiri; a chronogram in its prologue (“sang akuda suddha candrama”) gives Śaka 1079, 1157 CE — the paraphrase even yields the day, 6 September 1157. It became the basis of the Javanese and Balinese tradition of the great war.
details: Zoetmulder (Kalangwan, Indonesian ed. 1983, p. 340): Mpu Sedah composed a chronogram for the king “drawn by horses (the sun) and the pure moon” — sang akuda suddha candrama — yielding Śaka 1079 = 1157 CE; the epilogue tells that Mpu Panuluh was charged with writing the last part.

dates.label: 1157 CE (Śaka 1079), 6 September
dates.basis: chronogram in the prologue, read by Zoetmulder

name: Hariwangsa (Kakawin)
summary: Mpu Panuluh’s Old Javanese kakawin (12th c.) on Kṛṣṇa’s abduction of Rukmiṇī and the war with Jarāsandha, drawing on the Harivaṃśa tradition; edited by A. Teeuw (1950).

dates.label: 12th c.
dates.basis: court and poet as identified by Zoetmulder

sources.locator: chapter list and chapters on the work

name: Ghaṭotkacāśraya (Kakawin)
summary: Mpu Panuluh’s Old Javanese kakawin (12th c.) on Ghaṭotkaca’s help to Abhimanyu in winning his bride — an episode not found in the Sanskrit Mahābhārata.

dates.label: 12th c.
dates.basis: court and poet as identified by Zoetmulder

sources.locator: chapter list and chapters on the work

name: Kṛṣṇāyana (Kakawin)
summary: Mpu Triguṇa’s Old Javanese kakawin on Kṛṣṇa’s abduction of Rukmiṇī, written at the court of King Warsajaya (early 12th c.).

name: Wirāṭaparwa (Old Javanese prose)
summary: The Old Javanese prose rendering of the Mahābhārata’s Virāṭaparvan, made at the court of King Dharmawangsa Teguh; its epilogue records that it was recited before the king over a month, which Zoetmulder computes as 14 October–12 November 996 CE — one of the earliest dated works of Old Javanese literature.

dates.label: 14 October – 12 November 996

name: Agama Hindu Dharma (Balinese Hinduism)
summary: The Hindu religion of Bali (and of Hindu communities elsewhere in Indonesia), joining temple-centred Śaiva and Buddhist priestly ritual inherited from Java with local ancestor and village temple cults. Under Indonesia’s state requirement of monotheism, Balinese reformers recast it around Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa as one supreme God and secured its recognition by the Ministry of Religion around 1958–59; the Parisada Hindu Dharma was founded as its council in 1959, and “Agama Hindu Bali” became the national “Agama Hindu” in the 1960s.

dates.event: recognition by Indonesia’s Ministry of Religion
dates.label: c. 1958–1962
dates.basis: Picard’s history of the recognition campaign

limits: The dates of recognition and renaming are summarised from Picard’s title and reference works; the ministerial decrees were not consulted.

name: Parisada Hindu Dharma Indonesia
summary: The council of Indonesian Hindus, founded in Bali in 1959 as Parisada Dharma Hindu Bali and later renamed for the whole country, which standardises doctrine and represents Hinduism to the state.

name: Maharadia Lawana (Maranao)
summary: A Maranao epic song from the Lake Lanao region of Mindanao (Philippines) whose hero is Maharadia Lawana — Rāvaṇa — to whom the gods grant immortality; a local, Islamised telling of the Rāma story. Juan R. Francisco heard it sung by Maranao bards in 1968 and published an English rendering with the Maranao scholar Nagasura Madale (1969), arguing that the story reached the Philippines between the 17th and 19th centuries through Javanese and Malay contacts.

dates.event: recorded by Francisco from Maranao bards
dates.label: heard 1968; published 1969

limits: The plot and character correspondences were not checked against Francisco’s text in this round.
openQuestions: Reference summaries disagree on whether Maharadia Lawana is presented as a monkey-king or as the Rāvaṇa figure abducting the heroine; Francisco 1969 should be consulted.

name: Hinduism in Mauritius
summary: The Hindu traditions of Mauritius, brought by indentured labourers from Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Andhra and Maharashtra from the 1830s; Hindus are the largest religious group (about 48% in the 2022 census), the only Hindu plurality in Africa. Its signature observances are the Mahāśivarātri pilgrimage to Ganga Talao (Grand Bassin), Thaipusam and Tamil kāvaṭi, and the Bhojpuri Geet-Gawai.

name: Grand Bassin (Ganga Talao) pilgrimage
summary: The Mahāśivarātri pilgrimage of Mauritian Hindus, many walking from across the island carrying decorated kāṁvaṛ, to the crater lake Grand Bassin, renamed Ganga Talao and ritually linked with the Gaṅgā; the island’s largest Hindu festival and, for Eisenlohr, a “cultural touchstone” of Indo-Mauritian identity.

name: Indo-Caribbean Hinduism
summary: The Hinduism of the descendants of Indian indentured labourers in Trinidad and Tobago (from 1845), British Guiana/Guyana (from 1838) and Suriname (from 1873), largely of Bhojpuri-speaking north Indian origin: Sanātanī temple and pandit organisations, Rāmāyaṇ (Mānas) recitation and Rāmlīlā, Phagwah (Holī) and Divālī as public festivals. Guyana has the highest proportion of Hindus in the Western Hemisphere.

dates.event: arrival of the first indentured labourers in Trinidad (Fatel Razack, 30 May 1845)
dates.label: 30 May 1845

dates.event: indentured migration to the Caribbean (Guyana 1838 – c. 1917)

name: Sanatan Dharma Maha Sabha (Trinidad and Tobago)
summary: The largest Hindu organisation of Trinidad and Tobago, formed in 1952 when Bhadase Sagan Maraj merged two Sanātanī bodies; it runs some 150 mandirs, over fifty schools and broadcast media.

name: Rāmlīlā of Trinidad
summary: Open-air village performances of the Rāma story in Trinidad, based on Tulsīdās’s Mānas and staged by Indo-Trinidadian communities from the late nineteenth century, culminating in the burning of Rāvaṇa’s effigy around Dussehra.
limits: The date of the first Trinidad Rāmlīlā (often said to be the 1880s) was not verified.

name: Phagwah (Caribbean Holī)
summary: The Caribbean form of Holī among Indo-Guyanese, Indo-Trinidadians and Indo-Surinamese, named from the Bhojpuri month Phāgun, with chowtal singing and the throwing of coloured water (abeer); a public holiday in Guyana and Suriname.

name: Hinduism in Fiji
summary: The Hinduism of Indo-Fijians, descendants of indentured labourers brought to the sugar plantations between 1879 and 1916; about a quarter of Fiji’s population (24% in 2017). Rāmāyaṇ maṇḍalīs reciting the Mānas, Sanātanī and Ārya Samāj organisations and south Indian fire-walking are among its institutions; Kelly (1991) studies its colonial-era politics of virtue.

name: Hinduism in Malaysia
summary: The Hinduism of Malaysia’s Indian (mostly Tamil) community, about 6% of the population (2020), formed largely by nineteenth- and early twentieth-century labour migration to the plantations; its great public festival is Thaipusam at Batu Caves near Kuala Lumpur, with its 43-metre Murukaṉ statue.

name: Hinduism in South Africa
summary: The Hinduism of Indian South Africans, mainly in KwaZulu-Natal, descended chiefly from indentured labourers brought to Natal from 1860 to 1911 and from later “passenger” migrants; Tamil, Telugu, Hindi- and Gujarati-speaking traditions coexist, with fire-walking festivals for Draupadī and Kāvaṭi for Murukaṉ.

name: Hindu temple-building in Britain
summary: The growth of British Hindu congregations from converted houses and halls in the 1960s–70s, after migration from India and East Africa, to purpose-built temples such as the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir at Neasden (1995) and many regional and sectarian mandirs; the temples belong to the temple records, this record to the community movement.

name: Hindu temple-building in the United States
summary: The establishment of temples by Indian professionals who arrived after the 1965 Immigration Act — among the first the Ganesha temple of the Hindu Temple Society of North America in Flushing, New York, and the Sri Venkateswara temple at Penn Hills, Pittsburgh (both consecrated 1977) — often built by south Indian craftsmen on Āgamic plans and serving pan-Hindu congregations.

dates.basis: temple histories as summarised by Eck and Waghorne

limits: Which temple was “first” depends on definition (consecration, construction, earlier Vedanta Society buildings).

name: ISKCON (International Society for Krishna Consciousness)
summary: A Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava movement founded in New York on 13 July 1966 by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda, which spread the chanting of the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra, Caitanya’s theology and his own translations of the Gītā and Bhāgavata among Western converts and later the Indian diaspora; its headquarters are at Māyāpur, West Bengal. It holds Ratha Yātrās in cities worldwide.

name: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
summary: Bengali Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava teacher (1896–1977), initiated in the Gauḍīya Maṭh line of Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī, who sailed to New York in 1965 aged 69 and founded ISKCON in 1966; his English translations and commentaries on the Bhagavad Gītā, Bhāgavata Purāṇa and Caitanya Caritāmṛta became the movement’s scriptures.
